cards: By how much does the plasma volume increase in pregnancy, and when does it peak?
It increases by about 45% and peaks at 32–34 weeks.
By how much does the red cell mass increase, and what is the effect on haemoglobin?
It increases by about 25%. Because the plasma volume rises more, haemoglobin falls by dilution (physiological anaemia).
What is the mean corpuscular volume (MCV) in physiological anaemia of pregnancy?
The MCV is normal, because the fall in haemoglobin is caused by haemodilution and not by iron deficiency.
Which coagulation factors change in pregnancy?
Fibrinogen and factors VII, VIII and X increase; protein S decreases.
By how much does the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) increase in pregnancy?
About 4–6 times; the risk is highest after delivery.
Why is a fibrinogen level of 2 g/L a concern in postpartum haemorrhage?
The normal level at term is 4–6 g/L, so 2 g/L indicates consumption of clotting factors (DIC).
By how much does cardiac output increase in pregnancy?
By about 40%; most of the increase occurs by 20–24 weeks.
When is blood pressure lowest in pregnancy?
In mid-pregnancy (22–24 weeks); it returns to the booking level by term.
Which heart murmur is a normal finding in pregnancy?
A soft ejection systolic flow murmur. A diastolic murmur is never normal.
When does cardiac output reach a second peak?
Immediately after delivery, because blood returns to the circulation from the uterus (autotransfusion).
After 20 weeks the uterus compresses the inferior vena cava when the woman lies supine, causing dizziness and low blood pressure. It is relieved by left lateral tilt.
Which respiratory measurement does not change in pregnancy?
The respiratory rate. Tidal volume and minute ventilation increase by 40%.
What is the normal arterial pCO₂ in pregnancy?
30 mmHg (4 kPa), which is lower than the non-pregnant range of 35–45 mmHg. This is a compensated respiratory alkalosis.
Why does oxygen saturation fall rapidly in a pregnant woman during apnoea?
Functional residual capacity (FRC) falls by 20% and oxygen consumption rises by 20%.
By how much does the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) increase in pregnancy?
By about 50%; therefore serum creatinine, urea and urate fall.

Why is glycosuria common in pregnancy?
The filtered glucose load exceeds tubular reabsorption. It is therefore not diagnostic of diabetes.
Why is asymptomatic bacteriuria treated in pregnancy?
The ureters are dilated and urine flow is slow (stasis), so 20–30% of cases progress to pyelonephritis.
Which liver enzyme rises in normal pregnancy?
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) rises 2–4 times, because it is also produced by the placenta.
What does a raised ALT in the third trimester indicate?
It indicates disease, because ALT does not rise in normal pregnancy. The causes are obstetric cholestasis, AFLP, HELLP syndrome and hepatitis.
When does the placenta take over progesterone production?
At 8–10 weeks. Before this, the corpus luteum is essential.
Which hormone causes insulin resistance in the second half of pregnancy?
Human placental lactogen (hPL), together with cortisol and progesterone.
Why is TSH low in the first trimester?
Because hCG stimulates the TSH receptor.
Why is total T4 raised in pregnancy while free T4 remains normal?
Oestrogen doubles the level of thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG).
Brown pigmented patches on the face in pregnancy (melasma), which become darker with sun exposure.
What is the recommended weight gain in pregnancy for a woman with a normal BMI?
11.5–16 kg; the average gain is about 12.5 kg.
What does a sudden weight gain of 1 kg or more in one week suggest?
Fluid retention; pre-eclampsia should be considered.
Why does mitral stenosis often decompensate at 24–28 weeks?
Because cardiac output and plasma volume reach near-peak levels at this time.
Why is screening for gestational diabetes performed at 24–28 weeks?
Because the insulin resistance caused by placental hormones (hPL) appears at this time.
What are the positive (certain) signs of pregnancy?
Fetal heart sounds heard or fetal heart activity seen, a fetus seen on ultrasound, and fetal parts or movements felt by the examiner.

Why is urine cultured at the booking visit?

What is the purpose of the hand-held antenatal card?
It carries the dates, results and plan of care with the woman to every visit and to labour.
How many antenatal contacts does WHO recommend?

What is checked at every antenatal visit?

Which women need folic acid 5 mg daily?

What is the daily iron supplement in pregnancy?
30–60 mg of elemental iron with folic acid.
Which women are given aspirin, and at what dose?

What dose of calcium reduces the risk of pre-eclampsia?

How many doses of Td does a never-vaccinated woman receive in her first pregnancy?

Why are NSAIDs avoided after 30 weeks?

How much extra energy is needed in pregnancy?

Which danger signs should every pregnant woman know?
Vaginal bleeding, convulsions, severe headache, fever, severe pain, breathlessness, reduced fetal movements and leaking of fluid.

Which features make a pregnancy high risk?
Previous caesarean section, previous PPH, medical disease, twin pregnancy, age below 18 or 35 and above, blood pressure ≥ 140/90 mmHg and malpresentation.

What is the first advice for heartburn in pregnancy?
Small frequent meals, no late meals and raising the head of the bed; antacids may be used.
How is normal vaginal discharge in pregnancy distinguished from abnormal discharge?
Normal discharge is white, odourless and not itchy. An itchy, curd-like discharge suggests candidiasis.
What is the benefit of screening for and treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy?
It prevents pyelonephritis and preterm labour.
Why is SP not given in the first trimester?
It is an antifolate drug, so it carries a risk during organogenesis.
Why is a blood donor arranged before delivery?
